title: Plato’s hidden maker and the Word made flesh
source_text: Εἶτα μετὰ ταῦτα ὡς ἐπὶ ἐνεργέστερον διδάσκαλον τῶν θεολογίας πραγμάτων ἀναπέμπει ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ τὸν Πλάτωνα, παρατιθέμενος αὐτοῦ τὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ Τιμαίου λέξεις οὕτως ἐχούσας· „τὸν μὲν οὖν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς εὑρεῖν τε ἔργον καὶ εὑρόντα εἰς πάντας ἀδύνατον λέγειν.“ εἶτ᾿ ἐπιφέρει τούτοις λέγων· ὁρᾶτε ὅπως ζητεῖται θεοπρόποις καὶ ἀληθείας ὁδὸς, καὶ ὡς ᾔδει Πλάτων ὅτι ταύτῃ βῆναι πᾶσιν „ἀδύνατον.“ ἐπειδὴ δὲ τούτου χάριν ἐξηύρηται σοφοῖς ἀνδράσιν, ὡς ἂν τοῦ ἀκατονομάστου καὶ πρώτου λάβοιμέν τινα ἐπίνοιαν, διαδηλοῦσαν αὐτὸν ἢ τῇ συνθέσει τῇ ἐπὶ τὰ ἄλλα ἢ ἀναλύσει ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν ἢ ἀναλογίᾳ, τὸ ἄλλως ἄῤῥητον θέλων διδάξαι θαυμάσαιμι δ᾿ ἂν εἰ ἀκολουθῆσαι δυνήσεσθε. παντελῶς τῇ σαρκὶ ἐνδεδεμένοι καὶ μηδὲν καθαρὸν βλέποντες. μεγαλοφυῶς μὲν οὖν καὶ οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτως τὴν ἐκκειμένην λέξιν ὁ Πλάτων προφέρεται. ὅρα δὲ εἰ μὴ φιλανθρωπότερον ὁ θεῖος λόγος εἰσάγει τὸν „ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν“ θεὸν λόγον γινόμενον σάρκα, ἵνα εἰς πάντας δυνατὸς ᾖ φθάνειν ὁ λόγος, ὃν καὶ τὸν „εὑρόντα εἰς πάντας ἀδύνατον λέγειν“ φησὶν ὁ Πλάτων. Πλάτων μὲν οὖν λεγέτω „τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς ἔργον“ εἶναι „εὑρεῖν,“ „ἀδύνατον“ ἐμφαίνων εἶναι τῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ φύσει τὸ εὑρεῖν κατ᾿ ἀξίαν τὸν θεὸν, ἢ εἰ μὴ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν ἀλλ᾿ ἐπὶ πλεῖόν γε καὶ παρὰ τοὺς πολλούς· ὅπερ εἰ ἦν ἀληθὲς καὶ θεὸς κατ᾿ ἀλήθειαν εὕρητο Πλάτωνι ἤ τινι Ἑλλήνων. οὐκ (ἂν) ἄλλο τι ἔσεβον καὶ θεὸν ἐκάλουν καὶ προσεκύνουν, ἤτοι τοῦτον καταλιπόντες ἢ συμπαραλαμβάνοντες τὰ μὴ συμπαραληπτὰ τῷ τηλικούτῳ θεῷ· ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀποφαινόμεθα ὅτι οὐκ αὐτάρκης ἡ ἀνθρωπίνη φύσις ὁπωσποτανοῦν ζητῆσαι τὸν θεὸν καὶ εὑρεῖν αὐτὸν καθαρῶς, μὴ βοηθηθεῖσα ὑπὸ τοῦ ζητουμένου, εὑρισκομένου τοῖς ὁμολογοῦσι μετὰ τὸ παρ᾿ αὐτοὺς ποιεῖν ὅτι δέονται αὐτοῦ, ἐμφανίζοντος ἑαυτὸν οἷς ἂν κρίνῃ εὔλογον εἶναι ὀφθῆναι, ὡς πέφυκε θεὸς μὲν ἀνθρώπῳ γινώσκεσθαι ἀνθρώπου δὲ ψυχὴ ἔτι οὖσα ἐν σώματι γινώσκειν τὸν θεόν.
pass_a_gloss: Then after these, as to a more effective (ἐνεργέστερος) teacher of the things of theology (θεολογία), he refers us to Plato, setting beside (παρατίθημι) his words (λέξις) from the Timaeus running thus: "the maker (ποιητής) and father (πατήρ) of this all (τὸ πᾶν) to find (εὑρίσκω) is a task (ἔργον), and having found, impossible (ἀδύνατος) to say (λέγω) to all." Then he adds (ἐπιφέρω) to these, saying: "you see how the road (ὁδός) of truth also is sought (ζητέω) by god-speakers/seers (θεοπρόπος), and how Plato knew that to walk (βαίνω) this way is impossible for all. And since for the sake of this it has been found out (ἐξευρίσκω) by wise men, so that we might take some notion/conception (ἐπίνοια) of the unnameable (ἀκατονόμαστος) and first (πρῶτος), making him manifest (διαδηλόω) either by synthesis/composition (σύνθεσις) onto the other things, or by analysis (ἀνάλυσις) from them, or by analogy (ἀναλογία), wishing to teach (διδάσκω) what is otherwise unspeakable (ἄρρητος), I would wonder (θαυμάζω) if you will be able to follow (ἀκολουθέω), being wholly bound (ἐνδέω) to the flesh (σάρξ) and seeing (βλέπω) nothing pure (καθαρός)." Grandly (μεγαλοφυῶς) then and not contemptibly (εὐκαταφρονήτως) Plato puts forward (προφέρω) the set-out passage. But see whether the divine word (ὁ θεῖος λόγος) does not more humanely (φιλανθρωπότερον) introduce (εἰσάγω) God the Word, "in the beginning with God", becoming (γίνομαι) flesh, so that the Word may be able to reach (φθάνω) to all, which [Word] Plato also says one having found [cannot] say to all. Let Plato then say "the maker and father of this all" is "a task" to find, indicating (ἐμφαίνω) that it is "impossible" for human nature (φύσις) to find God according to worth (κατ' ἀξίαν), or if not according to worth, at least more and beyond (παρά) the many; which if it were true and God had truly been found by Plato or some of the Greeks, they would not revere (σέβω) something else and call it god and worship (προσκυνέω), either abandoning (καταλείπω) this one or taking along with (συμπαραλαμβάνω) things not to be taken along with so great a God. But we declare (ἀποφαίνομαι) that human nature is not sufficient (αὐτάρκης) in any way whatever (ὁπωσποτανοῦν) to seek God and find him purely (καθαρῶς), not helped (βοηθέω) by the one sought, found (εὑρίσκω) by those confessing (ὁμολογέω), after doing what is in their power, that they need (δέομαι) him, manifesting (ἐμφανίζω) himself to whom he judges (κρίνω) it reasonable (εὔλογος) to be seen (ὁράω), as it is natural (πέφυκε) for God to be known (γινώσκω) by man and for the soul (ψυχή) of man, still being in a body, to know God.
pass_b_english: Then, after this, he sends us back to Plato as to a more effective teacher of the things of theology, and sets out his words from the Timaeus, which run as follows: “Now to find the maker and father of this universe is a hard task, and having found him, it is impossible to declare him to all” (Plato, Timaeus 28c). Then he adds to these words, saying: “You see how the way of truth too is sought by seers, and how Plato knew that to walk this way is ‘impossible’ for all. But since, for this reason, wise men have devised a means by which we might grasp some idea of the Nameless and First, one that makes him plain either by synthesis applied to other things, or by analysis from them, or by analogy, and since I wish to teach what is otherwise beyond speech, I should be surprised if you were able to follow, bound as you are wholly to the flesh and seeing nothing pure.”

Plato, indeed, puts forward the passage set out above in a lofty way, and one not to be despised. But see whether the divine word does not show greater love for mankind when it presents God the Word, who was “in the beginning with God” (John 1:2), becoming flesh (John 1:14), so that the Word might be able to reach all: the very Word of whom Plato says that, for one who has found him, it is “impossible to declare him to all”.

Let Plato say, then, that “to find the maker and father of this universe” is “a hard task”, showing that it is “impossible” for human nature to find God as he deserves, or, if not as he deserves, at least more fully than the many do. If this were true, and God had in truth been found by Plato or by any of the Greeks, they would not have revered something else and called it god and bowed down to it, either abandoning him or taking alongside him things that may not be taken alongside so great a God.

But we declare that human nature is not sufficient in any way at all to seek God and find him purely, unless it is helped by the One it seeks. He is found by those who, after doing what lies in their power, confess that they need him, and he shows himself to those to whom he judges it reasonable to be seen (Wisdom of Solomon 1:2), so far as it is natural for God to be known by man, and for the soul of man, while it is still in a body, to know God.

choices.choice: Timaeus 28c quoted exactly; ἔργον rendered “a hard task” (the sense of ἔργον with an infinitive here). θεοπρόποις in Celsus: “seers” (men who declare divine things); the line is Celsus’s, not Plato’s. The Celsus quotation runs to βλέποντες; the participle θέλων διδάξαι is taken as Celsus speaking of himself (“since I wish to teach”). σύνθεσις / ἀνάλυσις / ἀναλογία: the three Middle Platonist ways to knowledge of the First (compare Alcinous, Didaskalikos 10); not cited inline as not quoted. ὁ θεῖος λόγος at the start of paragraph two is taken as “the divine word” (Scripture, lower case), as distinct from θεὸν λόγον, “God the Word”; Origen plays on λόγος (Word/speech) against Plato’s “impossible to declare (λέγειν)”. “in the beginning with God” quotes John 1:2 (cf. 1:1); λόγον γινόμενον σάρκα alludes to John 1:14. εὑρισκομένου ... ἐμφανίζοντος ἑαυτόν echoes Wisdom of Solomon 1:2 LXX (εὑρίσκεται τοῖς μὴ πειράζουσιν αὐτόν, ἐμφανίζεται δὲ τοῖς μὴ ἀπιστοῦσιν αὐτῷ): an echo of the pair of verbs, not a quotation. Koetschau’s supplement οὐκ (ἂν) accepted. Pronouns for God left lower case per house examples; “One it seeks” capitalised as a substantive for God. Review: Timaeus 28c checked word for word against the quoted Greek.
